blocks.text: The argument list is where a prompt template meets the messy reality of what a user actually typed, or forgot to type, or typed wrong.
Getting arguments right is the difference between a prompt that feels solid and dependable and one that quietly produces garbled output the moment something is missing.

This lesson is a deep dive on exactly that: what an argument is made of, the difference between required and optional, why prompt arguments stay deliberately simple as plain strings, and what a well behaved server does the moment a request comes in short or malformed.
1. Arguments Are the Parameters of a Prompt

blocks.alt: A prompt takes arguments the same way a function takes parameters

blocks.text: Every prompt argument plays the same role a function parameter plays in ordinary programming, it names one specific piece of information the template needs before it can be filled in correctly. Just as a function signature tells a caller what to pass and in what order, a prompt's argument list tells a client exactly what to collect from a user, or from elsewhere in the conversation, before calling prompts/get.

The comparison only goes so far, though. Prompt arguments are described for a human reading a description, not compiled and type checked the way a function signature is, which shapes almost everything else covered in this lesson.

blocks.title: A quick self-check
blocks.content: If you can name every value a specific prompt template needs to be filled in correctly, you understand its argument list.

blocks.text: 2. The Fields Each Argument Declares

Every argument in a prompt's declared list carries exactly three fields: a name, a description, and a required flag. That is the entire shape MCP defines for an argument, deliberately minimal compared to the rich JSON Schema a tool's input can carry.

code.content: {"name": "sentence_count", "description": "How many sentences the summary should have", "required": false}

blocks.text: 3. Required Arguments

blocks.alt: A required argument is compared against an optional argument

blocks.text: An argument marked required true is one the template genuinely cannot be filled in without. Leaving a required argument out of a prompts/get call is a client error, not a valid alternate path, and a well built server should refuse the request rather than attempt to guess or silently substitute something in its place.

A good habit when designing a new prompt is asking, for each candidate argument, "if this were left blank, would the resulting message still make sense?" If the honest answer is no, it belongs in the required list.
4. Optional Arguments

An argument marked required false, or with the required field simply omitted, is one the template can do without, either by falling back to a sensible default or by adjusting its own structure to leave out whatever depended on that value. Optional arguments are what let a single prompt serve both a quick, minimal use and a more detailed, fine tuned use without needing two separate prompt names.
An optional argument that is never supplied should fall back to a sensible, documented default rather than silently producing an incomplete or broken template.
5. Types: Why Prompt Arguments Are Just Strings

blocks.alt: Every prompt argument is passed as a plain string value

blocks.text: Unlike a tool's input schema, which can declare numbers, booleans, arrays, and deeply nested objects, a prompt argument has no formal type system at all beyond being a string. This is a deliberate simplification, not an oversight. Prompt arguments are meant to be things a person can type directly into a small text field in a chat client, and a person cannot type a JSON array into a text box any more naturally than they can type a plain sentence.

blocks.title: Strings all the way down
blocks.content: Even something conceptually numeric, like a year or a count, arrives as a string in a prompt argument. Any parsing or validation of that string into a stricter type happens entirely on the server.

blocks.text: This string only convention keeps the prompt argument format simple and consistent across every server, even when the underlying data being represented is genuinely structured.
6. Encoding Structured Data Inside a String Argument

Occasionally a prompt genuinely needs something more structured than a single word, a list of tags, a small set of key value pairs. Since the wire format only offers a string, the common approach is a simple, human writable convention, comma separated values, or a short line of key equals value pairs, described clearly in the argument's own description so a user knows exactly how to type it.

code.content: { "name": "tags", "description": "Comma separated tags to apply, e.g. urgent, billing, refund", "required": false }

blocks.text: If a piece of input truly needs deep, unambiguous structure, arrays of objects, nested fields, that is usually a sign the job belongs to a tool rather than a prompt, since tools carry a proper JSON Schema built exactly for that purpose.
7. Validating Arguments Before Filling the Template

When a prompts/get request arrives, a well behaved server checks it before doing any substitution: are all required arguments present, and does each value look reasonable given what the argument is supposed to represent. Only once this check passes should the server proceed to actually build the filled messages.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Check","Example failure"],"rows":[["Required present","Missing document_text"],["Type valid","sentence_count is not a number"]]}

blocks.text: 8. What Happens When a Required Argument Is Missing

blocks.alt: A missing required argument leads to an error rather than filling the template

blocks.text: A missing required argument should produce a clear, immediate error, not a template filled with a blank or a placeholder like "undefined" left sitting in the message text. Silently proceeding with missing data is worse than refusing outright, because it produces a plausible looking but subtly broken message that a user might not notice until it has already been sent to a model.
A server should reject the request clearly and immediately, rather than attempting to fill the template with a blank or placeholder value that would produce a confusing result.
9. What Happens When an Argument Value Is Invalid

Beyond simply being present, a value can also be present but wrong, a target_language argument holding "xyz123" instead of a real language name, for instance. Since prompt arguments carry no formal type constraint, catching this kind of problem is entirely up to whatever validation logic the server author chooses to write, ranging from no checking at all to a careful check against a known list of accepted values.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Situation","Reasonable server behavior"],"rows":[["Required argument missing entirely","Reject the request with a clear error"],["Optional argument missing","Use a documented default or omit the dependent clause"],["Argument present but clearly nonsensical","Reject with an error naming the problem, or fall back safely if low stakes"],["Argument present and well formed","Proceed to fill and return the template"]]}

blocks.text: Catching an invalid value before filling the template avoids producing a broken or nonsensical final message that would confuse the model receiving it.
10. Returning a Clear Error to the Client

When prompts/get fails validation, the server should return a proper JSON-RPC error, with a message specific enough that a client, or the human behind it, can understand exactly what needs to be fixed. "Invalid arguments" tells a user nothing useful, "Missing required argument: target_language" tells them exactly what to add.
11. Whose Job Is Validation: Client or Server

blocks.alt: Client side validation is compared against server side validation

blocks.text: The server is always the final authority on validation, since it is the party that actually knows what a valid value looks like and it is the one filling in the template.

A thoughtful client can offer a better user experience by checking obviously missing required fields before ever sending the request, sparing a round trip for an error that was entirely predictable, but that client-side check is a convenience layer, never a substitute for the server doing its own real validation.
The server should always validate, even if a well-behaved client already did, since a server can never fully trust that every caller performed its own checks correctly.
12. Defaults for Optional Arguments

A default is the value, or behavior, a server falls back on when an optional argument is left out. Good defaults are unsurprising, a tone argument left blank should probably default to something calm and neutral, not something wildly casual or wildly formal. Whenever a default exists, naming it directly in the argument's description saves a user from having to guess by trial and error.

code.content: sentence_count = arguments.get("sentence_count", 3)   # a sensible default when not supplied

blocks.text: 13. Argument Descriptions as Lightweight Documentation

Because there is no formal type system to lean on, an argument's description is doing more work in a prompt than a parameter's type annotation does in most programming languages. A good description states what the value represents, gives an example of an acceptable value, and, for optional arguments, states the default. Skimping on this text is one of the most common ways a perfectly reasonable prompt becomes confusing to use.
A short, specific description for each argument helps a client, or a human filling in a form, understand exactly what value is expected without needing to consult separate documentation.
14. Ordering and Grouping Arguments Sensibly

While MCP does not mandate any particular ordering for the arguments array, listing required arguments before optional ones, and grouping related arguments next to each other, makes a real difference to how a client renders a form for a human to fill in. A user scanning top to bottom should see the must-fill fields first, and the nice-to-have refinements after.
Listing required arguments before optional ones, and grouping related arguments together, makes a template noticeably easier for a human or client to fill in correctly.
15. Arguments vs Tool Input Schemas: A Deliberate Contrast

blocks.alt: Simple string arguments are compared against a full tool input schema

blocks.text: It is worth sitting with why MCP chose two different approaches for what looks like a similar problem, describing expected input. Tools are invoked by the model itself, often assembling structured input programmatically, so a rich JSON Schema with types, enums, and nesting pays for itself. Prompts are invoked by a person typing into a form, so a flat list of named strings with good descriptions serves that audience far better.

blocks.text: 16. Testing a Prompt's Argument Handling

blocks.alt: Testing a prompt means checking its argument handling with valid and invalid input

blocks.text: Before shipping a new prompt, it is worth deliberately calling prompts/get with each required argument missing one at a time, with an optional argument omitted, and with a clearly invalid value, and confirming the server responds the way you would want a user to experience it, a clear error in the first and third cases, a sensible default result in the second.

code.content:
# Manual test checklist for a prompt with arguments [source_text (required), target_language (required), tone (optional)]
# 1. Omit source_text -> expect a clear "missing required argument" error
# 2. Omit target_language -> expect a clear "missing required argument" error
# 3. Omit tone -> expect a successful fill using the documented default tone
# 4. Pass target_language="not_a_real_language" -> expect either a clear rejection or a documented graceful fallback

# testing a missing required argument
response = client.get_prompt("summarize_document", {})
assert "error" in response

blocks.text: 17. Evolving Arguments Without Breaking Existing Users

Adding a new optional argument to an existing prompt is safe, any client that has not been updated simply never sends it, and the server falls back to its default. Removing an argument, or changing a required argument to suddenly be mandatory when it previously was not, breaks any client still calling the old way. This topic is explored fully in the lesson on prompt versioning later in this module.
Adding a new optional argument is almost always safe, removing or renaming an existing one is far riskier and usually warrants the prompt versioning approach covered in the next lesson.
Worked Example

Consider a prompt named draft_apology_email with three arguments: customer_name, required, issue_description, required, and refund_offered, optional, defaulting to no mention of a refund at all if left out.

A client calling prompts/get with only customer_name and issue_description gets back a clean apology email with no mention of a refund. Calling it without issue_description at all should be rejected immediately with a clear error naming exactly that missing field.
Common Mistakes

items: Silently filling a template with an empty string when a required argument is missing instead of rejecting the request.
Writing an argument description that states its name again instead of explaining what value it expects.
Trying to smuggle deeply nested structured data into a single string argument instead of using a tool for that job.
Never stating what an optional argument defaults to, leaving users to guess by trial and error.
Skipping server-side validation entirely because the client is assumed to have already checked everything.
Marking an argument required when the template actually degrades gracefully without it.

blocks.text: A further common mistake is exposing an argument name that is unclear or cryptic, like arg1, instead of something descriptive like document_text.
Practice

Take the draft_apology_email prompt from the worked example and add a fourth optional argument, urgency, describing how soon a response is needed, with a sensible default. Write the full arguments array, and then write out what a prompts/get error response should look like if issue_description is left out.
As a final check, verify that supplying an unexpected extra argument the template does not use is handled gracefully rather than causing an error.
Key Takeaway

A prompt's arguments are its parameters, each one named, described, and marked required or optional, always represented as a plain string with no formal type system behind it. The server is responsible for validating what actually arrives, rejecting clearly with a specific error when something required is missing or invalid, and falling back sensibly on documented defaults when an optional value is left out.
The next lesson turns to prompts/list itself, the method a client uses to discover what prompts a server offers in the first place, before any argument ever gets filled in.
